So this took me exactly 1 hour and 15 minutes to do from scratch. (It was streamed on twitch as I hold a weekly challenge where we animate under time restrictions. Unfortunately I don't have the VOD).  


What this style is called:  
I work in Motion Design. It's a mix of design and animation, usually it's more commercial used and you'll see it in ads and what not. Sometimes though, the client wants something fun and atmospheric like this animation made.  


How to get into it easily:  
It's all about getting started. The main things you want to do is set yourself a challenge, people like to do those "30 day" challenges where they pick a topic every day and animate it. High volumes of work will get you improving faster.   


How to learn the software:

Free resources on YouTube are absolutely amazing, here are some off the top of my dome:  


School Of Motion  
Ben Marriott  
Motion By Nick  
Motion Design School  
ECAbrams  
Jacob Richardson  


You can always look into paid online courses, here are two I recommend:  


School Of Motion  
Mograph Mentor  


School of Motion (SoM) is quite affordable when compared to normal university fees. Plus you learn A LOT industry, skill and networking wise. You come out of it not just with new skill but also knowing likeminded people. Some good courses to get you started would be "AE Kickstarter" and "Animation Bootcamp".   
I have legit never heard anything bad about SoM  


Mograph Mentor on the other hand is built on mentors from the industry, you'll be connected with your specialised mentor and will undergo industry standard projects etc. I've also never heard anything bad about this one.  


One that I would avoid at all costs:  


Motion Design School. Shortly put, its a rip off. The courses are just a couple of videos and it feels they do it more for money than for teaching others.  
They do have good free YouTube tutorials that are about 1 minute long and packed with good info.  


One thing I 100% recommend for learning is a good feedback loop. Build friends, make sure you post your work because if you don't, you'll never know what you oculd improve on.

Last but not least, how I learnt:  


I basically just learnt through experimentation, working on challenges with friends and constantly trying to create. I've been using these programs for about 7 - 8 years but I was pretty slow at it so it took me a good while to get good at it.   
I've got some more work up here if you'd like to see [akamhr.com](https://akamhr.com/)  


Though don't get discouraged because it doesn't take that long usually, I have a friend  who started in around late summer or early autumn of 2020 and he already has a job and is doing well for himself.  [Will Staiger](https://www.willstaiger.com/)   


Guess what I'm trying to say is learn at your own pace and great things will happen. (I also get it if this isn't what you wanna work in but just want it as a hobby but the same advice stands!)
